steps.title: A turning world
steps.instruction: Sunrise is a moving boundary between darkness and daylight. We'll follow it from a marked place.

steps.title: Find London
steps.instruction: Look at London on the globe. Notice which side faces the Sun. The marker and the daylight calculation are separate clues.

steps.title: Predict the direction
steps.instruction: As Earth spins eastward, which way does the dawn boundary move across a map of longitudes?
steps.right: Yes. At a fixed UTC time, the dawn line moves westward over longitudes as Earth rotates east.
steps.wrong: It moves westward across longitudes. Earth itself turns eastward, carrying each place into daylight.

steps.title: Advance the scene
steps.instruction: Move the globe's lesson clock forward two hours and watch the light shift. This is a simulation, while Today stays real-time.

steps.title: What changed?
steps.instruction: The sunlight direction changed with time. Did the saved place move on the globe?
options: No; Earth rotated relative to the Sun
steps.right: Exactly. The place keeps its coordinates while Earth's rotation changes its illumination.
steps.wrong: A place keeps its latitude and longitude. The changing angle to the Sun creates day and night.

steps.title: A pattern around the Pacific
steps.instruction: Visit three locations, predict a pattern, then reveal plate boundaries. Historical fallback examples are labelled with dates and sources.

steps.title: Off Japan
steps.instruction: Historical fallback: 2011-03-11 Tohoku earthquake, USGS. A recent Pacific observation is used when available.

steps.title: The Cascades
steps.instruction: Historical fallback: 1980-05-18 Mount St. Helens eruption, USGS. This is a dated lesson example, not a live report.

steps.title: Along Chile
steps.instruction: Historical fallback: 1960-05-22 Great Chilean earthquake, USGS. This example stays outside the live-events repository.

steps.title: What pattern do you see?
steps.instruction: Which broad pattern links many earthquake and volcano locations around the Pacific?
options: A belt near several plate edges
One straight line through the Pacific center
Every event lies exactly on one boundary
steps.right: Yes. Many cluster near plate edges, but some events also happen away from mapped boundaries.
steps.wrong: The broad pattern is a belt near several plate edges. Individual events need their own evidence; distance to a line is not a diagnosis.

steps.title: Reveal the boundaries
steps.instruction: Gold lines show a generalized PB2002 plate-boundary model. Compare the Pacific rim; these lines do not explain every individual event.

steps.title: What the pattern means
steps.instruction: Plate motions concentrate many earthquakes and volcanoes around the Pacific. Hotspots and earthquakes within plates show why the pattern has exceptions.

steps.title: Two hemispheres
steps.instruction: Compare daylight at London and Sydney on two dates. Earth's tilted axis changes how long the Sun stays above the horizon.

steps.title: London in June
steps.instruction: Observe London near the June solstice. The Northern Hemisphere has longer daylight.

steps.title: Sydney in June
steps.instruction: Observe Sydney on the same date. Its winter daylight is shorter than London's summer daylight.

steps.title: Predict December
steps.instruction: Near the December solstice, which marked place has longer daylight?
steps.right: Yes. The Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun in December, so Sydney has longer days.
steps.wrong: Sydney has longer daylight near the December solstice. The Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun then.

steps.title: Switch to December
steps.instruction: Compare the daylight readouts after changing the lesson date. This changes the app scene only.

steps.title: Why seasons change
steps.instruction: Earth's axis stays tilted about 23.4° as it orbits the Sun. The Northern and Southern Hemispheres alternate longer daylight. The visible guides mark the equator, tropics, and polar circles.
